author: AI/search_experience_root_author
reviewScope: Independent language, selected-sense scope, bounded aliases/forms, and bilingual example fidelity. No reference examples copied into product content; no whole-dictionary quality claim.

reviewedRows.reason: Noun phrase for critical synthesis of prior research, not a bare reference list. The comparison-of-explanations example is faithful in Chinese.
reviewedRows.aliasAndFormReason: Regular reviews plural only; both Chinese aliases mean the research genre.

reviewedRows.reason: Noun phrase for permitted baggage limits. Emirates confirms weight and piece concepts and dimensional limits with route/fare variation. The example makes no fixed allowance promise.
reviewedRows.aliasAndFormReason: Only allowances plural; aliases are limits, not excess-baggage fees.

reviewedRows.reason: Noun phrase for travel away from the departure point, contrasted here with the return leg. Cambridge outbound confirms direction; train outward and bus return are preserved.
reviewedRows.aliasAndFormReason: Only journeys plural; aliases mean the outward leg, not all departures.

reviewedRows.reason: Verb phrase using book to arrange a future service; the selected advance-reservation sense is accurate. Six-in-the-morning taxi and the first train arriving too late align in both languages.
reviewedRows.aliasAndFormReason: books/booked/booking inflect book correctly. Chinese aliases are reservations, not hailing a passing taxi.

reviewedRows.reason: Abstract noun phrase for everyday financial self-support. Cambridge financially independent confirms not needing money from others. The source expressly distinguishes retirement-without-work meanings. Example and translation align.
reviewedRows.aliasAndFormReason: No artificial plural; aliases retain financial self-reliance.

reviewedRows.reason: Transitive verb phrase. Oxford and Cambridge confirm the memory-learning sense and British memorise spelling. The personal-sentence learning example is faithfully translated.
reviewedRows.aliasAndFormReason: All seven bounded spelling/inflection surfaces are valid; no reminisce sense is substituted.

reviewedRows.reason: Verb phrase for beginning employment, not necessarily orientation or paperwork. Cambridge start explicitly documents this use. Omar and the notebook of unfamiliar procedures are preserved in Chinese.
reviewedRows.aliasAndFormReason: starts/started/starting are correct. 入职 is explicitly scoped to commencing work.

reviewedRows.reason: Verb phrase using wear for having a mask on. Cambridge confirms the protective nose-and-mouth mask. Other face-mask senses are acknowledged without conflating them. Crowded-train example and translation align.
reviewedRows.aliasAndFormReason: wears/wore/worn/wearing are valid verb surfaces; participles are not claimed as independent full sentences.

reviewedRows.reason: Verb phrase for obtaining sufficient sleep. Cambridge sleep confirms the collocation. The example is a personal concentration observation preserved in Chinese, not a medical guarantee.
reviewedRows.aliasAndFormReason: gets/got/getting and American participle gotten are valid. Chinese aliases mean sufficient sleep.

reviewedRows.reason: Countable noun phrase for an airport registration counter; Cambridge check-in supports the airport area/process. The moved-counter example remains a location change in both languages.
reviewedRows.aliasAndFormReason: Regular counters plural; aliases remain airport-specific.

reviewedRows.reason: Countable noun phrase. Airport and hotel check-in contexts are explicitly separated. The room-key example clearly selects the hotel reading and translates it without adding a flight.
reviewedRows.aliasAndFormReason: Regular desks plural. Two Chinese aliases distinguish airport and hotel settings.

reviewedRows.reason: Idiomatic phrase for shared understanding or broad agreement on the relevant matter; Cambridge page confirms shared ideas. Source avoids universal agreement. The deadline example remains issue-specific in Chinese.
reviewedRows.aliasAndFormReason: No speculative variants; Chinese aliases mean shared understanding.

reviewedRows.reason: Idiom with distinct help and applause readings; Cambridge hand documents both. The example clearly selects practical help moving a desk, faithfully reflected in Chinese.
reviewedRows.aliasAndFormReason: Seven bounded pronoun/placeholder forms are grammatical. No claim that lend shares the applause reading.

reviewedRows.reason: Help idiom; Cambridge give-a-hand explicitly lists lend someone a hand. Applause is correctly absent. The heavy-box example and Chinese搬 retain the practical-help context.
reviewedRows.aliasAndFormReason: Seven bounded pronoun/placeholder forms retain assistance, not financial lending or applause.

reviewedRows.reason: Idiom with separately numbered unexamined-assumption and failure-to-value senses, both confirmed directly by Merriam-Webster. The Sunday-library example and Chinese select the first sense.
reviewedRows.aliasAndFormReason: takes/took/taken/taking are correct bounded forms; it is retained. No literal permission or donation sense is added.

reviewedRows.reason: Noun denoting an access event or identity credentials, confirmed by Dictionary.com and Cambridge. Two-word log in is correctly recommended as the verb. The office-computer event is preserved in Chinese.
reviewedRows.aliasAndFormReason: logins and hyphenated log-in/log-ins are valid noun surfaces. No invented loginned/loginning. The inaccessible Chicago FAQ is not relied on.

referenceLimitations: Several Cambridge direct fetches returned 403; first-party dictionary search-index text was read instead. Chicago FAQ direct fetch returned 500 and is not evidence for this approval. Dictionary.com and Cambridge independently support login. The removed by a fluke row is not approved.
